summary.text: The Bay of Fundy is an arm of the Atlantic Ocean between New Brunswick and Nova Scotia in Canada, with a small part touching Maine.
Tidal resonance in its funnel-shaped basin gives it the highest tidal range in the world, averaging about 16 metres.
In one half-day tide about 100 billion tonnes of water flows in and out, twice the combined flow of all the world's rivers over that time.

facts.label: How it formed
facts.value: A rift basin from the breakup of Pangaea

facts.label: Fossil highlight
facts.value: Canada's oldest dinosaur fossil, at Burntcoat Head

items.prompt: The world's tides rise and fall about one metre on average. Roughly how does the Bay of Fundy compare?

options.label: Roughly twice as large
About 16 times as large
About 100 times as large
About the same size

items.explain: Fundy's tidal range is about 16 metres, while the average range worldwide is only about one metre.

items.prompt: What makes the Bay of Fundy's tides so extreme?

options.label: Strong winds that blow up the bay
Many large rivers pouring into it
Its funnel shape makes the water resonate
The Moon passes closest to Canada

items.explain: Tidal resonance in the funnel-shaped basin produces both the huge range and very powerful tidal flows.

items.prompt: As the tide pours in, what happens on many of the rivers that drain into the Bay of Fundy?

options.label: They briefly dry up near the mouth
Their seaward flow speeds up sharply
Their water turns fresh far out to sea
A wave front pushes upstream against them

items.explain: Most of these rivers have a tidal bore, a wave front of the incoming tide that travels up the river against its normal flow.

items.prompt: A causeway built across the Petitcodiac River was followed by silt filling the channel. What happened to its large tidal bore?

options.label: It shrank, then came back once the gates opened
It grew into the largest bore in the world
It moved over to a neighbouring river
It stayed the same as before the build

items.explain: The bore had been one of the world's largest before the causeway and siltation; after the gates opened in 2010 it began returning.

items.prompt: How did the basin that holds the Bay of Fundy first form?

options.label: A meteorite struck and left a crater
A volcano collapsed into the sea
Rifting as the supercontinent Pangaea split
Rivers wore it down over millions of years

items.explain: As Pangaea broke up, rifting created a series of rift basins along eastern North America, including the Fundy Basin.

items.prompt: Water around the bay's mudflats carries very large amounts of fine sediment. What puts it there?

options.label: Tidal turbulence eroding old sedimentary rock
Dust storms blowing in from the land
Waste washed out of nearby towns
Meltwater from glaciers upstream

items.explain: Tidal turbulence keeps the water loaded with fine sediment eroded from Carboniferous and Triassic sedimentary rock.

paragraphs.heading: Where it is
paragraphs.text: The Bay of Fundy lies between two Canadian provinces, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, with a small part reaching the US state of Maine. It branches off the Gulf of Maine and belongs to the Atlantic Ocean.

paragraphs.heading: A flood of water
paragraphs.text: In a single half-day tide, around 100 billion tonnes of water pour in and out of the bay. That is double what every river on Earth carries, all added together, over the same stretch of time, and the currents it makes are very powerful. A 20 MW tidal power plant, the Annapolis Royal Generating Station on the Annapolis River, ran until it shut down in 2019. It was among a handful of tidal plants worldwide, and North America's only one.

paragraphs.heading: What the name means
paragraphs.text: The Mi'kmaq and Passamaquoddy peoples called the bay Bakudabakek, meaning open way. The Wolastoqiyik called it Wekwabegituk, waves at the head of the bay. Fundy itself may come from the French fendu, split, or from Fond de la Baie, head of the bay. Others, including William Francis Ganong, have argued for a Portuguese origin linked to João Álvares Fagundes.

paragraphs.heading: Born when a continent split
paragraphs.text: About 220 million years ago, in the late Triassic, all land formed one supercontinent, Pangaea, and today's Maritimes sat near the equator in a warm tropical climate. As Pangaea broke apart, rifting opened a chain of basins along eastern North America, the Fundy Basin among them. Lava erupted during the breakup and cooled into basalt, including the column-shaped rock seen on Brier and Grand Manan islands. Sediment later filled the rifts and hardened into sedimentary rock.

paragraphs.heading: Fossils and wildlife
paragraphs.text: The shoreline is rich in fossils: Canada's oldest dinosaur fossil came from Burntcoat Head, and very early reptiles were found inside Carboniferous tree trunks at Joggins. The bay belongs to UNESCO's Global Geoparks Network. Whales feed here, including the critically endangered North Atlantic right whale, so in 2003 the Canadian Coast Guard moved shipping lanes to cut the risk of collisions. In the Minas Basin, mudflats stretch as much as 4 km between the low and high water marks.
